newsitem.title: USA: Dollar rises on rate hopes, budget plan.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rises on rate hopes, budget plan.

text.p: The dollar rose against the German mark and Swiss franc Monday on hopes for higher interest rates in the United States and enthusiasm over an agreement to balance the federal budget in five years.

The dollar edged lower against other major currencies. But the moves came in thin trading and were not all that significant because financial markets in Tokyo and London were closed for holidays, traders and analysts said.

With no fresh economic data to guide them, traders looked to a Labour Department report on Friday for signs that Federal Reserve policy-makers may raise rates again when they meet on May 20 to keep the economy from growing too rapidly.
Although the report showed the economy added a moderate 142,000 jobs in April, it also said the April unemployment rate fell to 4.9 percent, the lowest level since 1973.

Fed policy-makers raised the federal funds rate, which banks charge one another for short-term loans, a quarter point on March 25. Higher domestic rates typically make dollar-based investments more attractive.
"I would be very surprised if they didn't raise (interest rates) in May," said Stephen Jury, chief dealer of foreign exchange at Union Bank of Switzerland.
Jury said the recent gains in the stock market give the Fed "even more confidence to go ahead and hike rates."
The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 142.48 points to 7,213.68, a record, in late trading.
The dollar rose to 1.7325 marks in late New York trading from 1.7293 marks late on Friday and to 1.4747 Swiss francs from 1.4710 francs.
The dollar edged lower to 126.54 Japanese yen from 126.62 yen and to Canadian $1.3803 from C$1.3807. The pound inched up to $1.6230 from $1.6220.

The federal budget deal also announced Friday remained in the spotlight amid Monday's dearth of economic data. The budget plan included a net tax cut of $85 billion, but a major part of the savings required to shrink the deficit would be found in the Medicare health care programme for the elderly, which would see a $115 billion reduction. Cuts in taxes and spending would be spread out over five years.

"I think the feeling with the U.S. is, especially in the short-term anyway, it's been helpful to the dollar because it's spread out over such a long period of time that it's not going to provide much of a retard to U.S. economic growth," said John Rothfield, economist at Nationsbanc.
"It'll free up some resources for higher private-sector growth," Rothfield added.
Markets in Tokyo were closed for the Children's Day holiday, and Britons enjoyed a bank holiday Monday. Trading in Tokyo and London will resume Tuesday.
Not surprisingly, traders described volume in the foreign exchange market as very light and warned that movements in exchange rates could be magnified.
"With two of the major three treasury centres closed for the day, any move should be exaggerated," said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Sakura Bank Ltd. in New York.
